"""
How level-0 players behave, and how they are perceived by higher-level players, are central questions in the literature on level-k models of boundedly rational strategic reasoning. These models distinguish between two conceptually and empirically distinct constructs, which we define and operationalize separately:

**Definitions**

- **Level-0 Actions (Behavioral):** These are the actual choices made by teams under explicit instructions *not* to strategize about others’ behavior. **Positively**, a level-0 action is defined as a choice reflecting a direct response to the set of options and payoffs—guided by the most obvious or prominent (i.e., “salient”) features—*without* any reference, explicit or implicit, to beliefs or predictions about other players’ likely choices. **Negatively**, any action referencing another agent’s (real or hypothetical) likely move, or predicated on “beating” or adjusting to others, is not level-0.  
  - *Example (level-0):* “We picked 50 because it is the midpoint.”  
  - *Example (not level-0):* “We picked 33 because others will pick 50, so 2/3×50=33.”
- **Level-0 Beliefs (Expectational):** These are teams’ stated *aggregate expectations* of how other, similarly non-strategic teams (under the same constraints) will behave. **Positively**, a level-0 belief is an explicit forecast about the *distribution* of choices likely to be selected by other non-strategic teams, *excluding* any belief about the members of one’s own team or about teams using strategic reasoning.  
  - *Example (level-0 belief):* “Most other level-0 teams will choose 20 because it is the highest.”  
  - *Example (not level-0 belief):* “Others might try to outguess, so I expect lower numbers.”

These definitions clarify that “action” is a decision absent beliefs about others, while “belief” refers to a forecast about similarly naïve decision-makers, both strictly non-iterative.

**Clarifying "Salience": Criteria for Coding**

A “salient” feature, for coding purposes, is an attribute that stands out perceptually (e.g., centrality in a range, largest or smallest value), structurally (e.g., endpoints, focal numbers, round numbers), or is made prominent by the payoff structure (e.g., highest base payoff, zero penalty). Coders identified salience using the following concrete criteria:
- The choice corresponds to a range endpoint (e.g., 20 in 11–20 game, 0 or 100 in beauty contest).
- The choice is the midpoint or “center” of the option range (e.g., 50 in 0–100 range).
- The number is structurally unique or perceptually focal (e.g., round numbers, default values).
- The justification refers to ease of selection, visual prominence, or explicit mention of “standing out,” “obviousness,” or “uniqueness” of the number.
A full checklist used by coders, with more detailed flags for salience identification, is provided in Appendix A.

**Operationalization**

In this study, **level-0 actions** are the choices teams make as a unit (after intra-team discussion but explicitly instructed to avoid reasoning about others), while **level-0 beliefs** are separately elicited forecasts by each team about the distribution of choices they expect other non-strategic teams to make under identical instructions. These two constructs are measured and coded independently on separated tasks for each team to avoid cross-contamination. All procedures, measurements, and codings are performed at the *team* (not individual) level.

**Coding Protocol and Reliability**

*Sample Description:* There were 25 teams in total (50 participants): 14 teams participated in the beauty contest, and 11 teams in the 11–20 game. All teams and game assignments were determined by random draw. Randomization was used for session order; task presentation was counterbalanced to mitigate order effects.

*Coding Rubric Adaptation:* Coding proceeded according to an explicit rubric, adapted from Burchardi & Penczynski (2014) and Goeree et al. (2018), with significant extensions for clarity and replicability. Changes included (1) a more detailed specification of positive and negative criteria for “salience,” (2) explicit boundaries for what counts as referencing others, (3) introduction of coder checklists for ambiguous cases, and (4) new illustrative edge-case examples drawn from this sample’s data. The full rubric, as well as calibration clarifications and justifications for modifications, are in Appendix A.

| Criterion                              | Yes (Level-0) Example                                                 | No (Non-Level-0) Example                                            |
|-----------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Absence of strategic/iterated reasoning | “We picked 50 because it’s the center.”                               | “We picked 33 because others will pick 50, so 2/3×50=33.”           |
| Reliance on salient features            | “20 is the largest possible number.”                                  | “We expect others to pick 18, so we pick 17 to go lower.”           |
| Payoff structure without iteration      | “20 is the safest and highest.” (“Safe”: maximal without penalty)     | “We chose 18 to beat average strategies.”                           |
| No explicit probabilistic/statistical talk | “This number stands out.”                                          | “Statistically, the average will be near 17.”                       |

Ambiguous justifications—e.g., “Pick 17, it just feels right”—were brought to coder discussion. If any reference (direct or indirect) to others was present, the decision was coded as non-level-0. Coders were trained with “edge” cases and standardized procedures. The process for resolving disagreements was as follows: Initial ratings were performed independently; initial agreement rates (pre-discussion) were 84%. When disagreements arose, coders discussed until consensus, with the protocol providing that if consensus could not be reached after discussion, a third-party arbitrator (a lead coder not involved in initial coding) would cast a deciding vote. This was needed in 2 out of 25 cases (8%). Final percent agreement (post-resolution) was 92%, with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.88, indicating high reliability.

**Tables and Figures**

- **Table 1** (included in the main text) reports anonymized sample justifications by coding category. Panel A shows typical level-0 beauty contest reasoning (“50 is in the middle and stands out”); Panel B presents 11–20 game justifications (“20 is the safest and highest; maximizing base payoff”); Panel C includes rare cases of action-belief divergence (e.g., “Action: safest choice for payoff; Belief: others may be more conservative”).
- **Figure 1** (included in the main text): Panel A displays histograms for team-level actions and beliefs in the beauty contest (responses cluster sharply at ~50); Panel B does the same for the 11–20 game (responses cluster near 20, avoiding minimum values); Panel C highlights outlier sessions where actions and beliefs diverged. All figures are based on team-level responses; corresponding tables and figures are available in the manuscript and are available for reader verification.

**Experimental Contexts**

1. **Beauty Contest (Burchardi & Penczynski, 2014):** Teams choose a number from 0–100; the winner is closest to two-thirds of the group average. Prior work finds level-0 actions often cluster at salient values (such as 50, the midpoint).
2. **11–20 Game (Goeree et al., 2018):** Teams select an integer 11–20, earn that number in base payoff, and a bonus for being uniquely lowest. Level-0 behaviors favor endpoints or payoff-salient numbers—not randomization.

**Quantitative Results**

In the beauty contest, for the 14 teams classified as level-0:
- **Mean action:** 51.2 (SD = 7.1, 95% CI [46.7, 55.7])
- **Mean level-0 belief:** 49.8 (SD = 7.9, 95% CI [44.7, 54.9])
- **Divergence:** Only one team deviated by more than 10 from the midpoint; most clustered at or near 50.
- **Refer to Table 1, Panel A** for representative justifications.

In the 11–20 game, among 11 level-0 teams:
- **Mean action:** 18.7 (SD = 1.6, 95% CI [17.8, 19.6]); modal response: 20 (5 teams); no team chose 11; remainder chose 17–19.
- **Mean level-0 belief:** 19.1 (SD = 1.3, 95% CI [18.3, 19.9])
- **Refer to Table 1, Panel B** for representative reasoning.

**Action–Belief Differences:** Across both games, divergence between action and belief was rare. In only 2 out of 25 sessions (8%) did action and belief differ by more than 6 units—a difference set a priori as substantively meaningful given the observed dispersion of team choices. Most differences were within ±2 units.
